newsitem.title: UK: UK junior minister criticised in official report.
newsitem.headline: UK junior minister criticised in official report.

text.p: The powerful Standards and Privileges Committee of Britain's parliament on Wednesday criticised junior minister David Willetts, saying he had been guilty of "dissembling", or seeking to conceal information, sources told the Press Association news agency.
The report is not officially due out until 1530 GMT, although Willetts was due to receive a copy two hours earlier.

The criticism is likely to be seized on by the opposition Labour party, riding high in opinion polls with just five months at most to an election, who have been demanding Willetts' resignation as a minister.

The report follows a two-month inquiry into Willetts' role in a row over allegations a former minister took cash and favours in return for asking parliamentary questions on behalf of Mohammed Al Fayed, the owner of London's top store, Harrods.
Hamilton and another minister, Tim Smith, quit after the allegations surfaced in the media. But Hamilton claimed he was innocent and started a libel action.
The current inquiry was launched after a document written by Willetts came to light in legal papers after Hamilton finally dropped his libel case against the Guardian newspaper which broke the story.
The committee was investigating whether Willetts, when he was a "whip", or government business manager, improperly tried to influence another panel of members of parliament probing Hamilton.
The central question of whether there was a cover-up of sleaze claims has considerable potential to embarrass Major in the run-up to a general election he must call by next May.

The televised hearings of the standards and privileges committee made front-page news in Britain last month after Willetts was accused by fellow Conservative MP Quentin Davies of deceiving the committee.
Davies said Willetts had changed his account of a meeting in 1994 with the chairman of the Hamilton committee to protect the latter from embarrassment.
Willetts, whose career could be ruined if he is judged to have deliberately misled MPs, told the committee: "There is no truth in the suggestion that I lied to this committee."
